I’m still capable of the work—I want to be clear about that—but the situation has made it very hard to keep up the way I used to.\n\nDoctor: About how long has this been going on?\n\nPatient: It’s been about 11 months now, roughly. Yes. I mean… I wouldn’t call them “messages” in some mystical sense, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like I think the television is speaking to me personally or anything like that. But ordinary things in the building—comments, noises, mail—yes, I’ve felt they were directed at me, because the pattern is too consistent to ignore.

They can show me paperwork or give explanations, and I understand what explanations are supposed to do, but paperwork doesn’t erase the pattern I’m seeing. It feels like pressure. Like they want me out, but they’re doing it indirectly so it can be denied.

I know how this sounds, but I’ve worked in management analysis for years—I notice patterns, I’m not just imagining connections out of nowhere. That’s really why I came in, because I need someone to understand what’s been happening.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe for certain that your neighbors and property manager are deliberately trying to force you out of your apartment?\n\nPatient: Yes. I mean, “for certain” is a strong phrase, but yes—I believe it because it’s not one thing in isolation. If it were just one piece of mail, or one odd noise, or one neighbor saying something strange, then fine, maybe I’d say it was coincidence. But this has been going on for months.\n\nThe mail gets misdelivered in ways that don’t make sense, the noises in the walls happen at very specific times, and then certain neighbors make these little comments—nothing openly threatening, but close enough to what’s been happening that it feels intentional. And every time I raise it, the property manager has some explanation, some paperwork, some reason it was a mistake or maintenance or whatever. But the explanations don’t change the overall pattern.\n\nSo yes, I think they’re deliberately trying to pressure me out of the apartment without coming out and saying it directly. That’s what it looks like to me.\n\nDoctor: Have you heard voices when no one else was there?\n\nPatient: No, not in the way you mean, I don’t think so. I haven’t had, like, a voice speaking to me in an empty room or giving me instructions or anything like that.\n\nWhat I have noticed is more—well, actual sounds in the building, things through the walls, hallway sounds, people talking somewhere nearby. If I hear something, I usually assume there’s a source for it, even if I can’t see the person at that moment.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that other people can somehow know your thoughts?\n\nPatient: I wouldn’t say they can read my thoughts, no. That’s what I keep trying to explain. It’s not mind reading. It’s people using the building and these little incidents to pressure me out without saying it openly.\n\nDoctor: Aside from what’s happening with your apartment, have you had any experiences that felt clearly strange or hard to explain, like something outside of yourself controlling or influencing you?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think so—not like something outside of me controlling me, if that’s what you mean. I don’t feel like my movements are being controlled, or that some force is putting thoughts into me, or anything like that.\n\nI mean, I do feel influenced in the ordinary sense that anyone would be influenced if they were under pressure for months—if things keep happening around your home, you start adjusting what you do, when you leave, how you respond. But that’s not the same as being controlled from outside myself. I still feel like my thoughts are my own and my decisions are my own.\n\nSo… aside from the apartment situation, I can’t think of anything clearly strange like that. If you mean something more specific, you might have to explain what kind of experience you’re asking about.\n\nDoctor: Has this situation made it hard for you to keep up with your work?\n\nPatient: Yes. It’s more like I’m lying there thinking, going over things, trying to remember what was said or what happened earlier, and then the next day I’m tired and slower, not full of energy.\n\nI haven’t had a stretch where I felt like I suddenly didn’t need sleep or was on top of the world or anything like that. It sounds like a lot, but if you don’t stay on top of it, they just smooth it over and make it seem like nothing.\n\nSo instead of sitting down to do my normal work, or even painting, which is usually how I settle myself, I end up spending hours on the apartment situation. I’m still capable of the work—I want to be clear about that—but the situation has made it very hard to keep up the way I used to.\n\nDoctor: About how long has this been going on?\n\nPatient: It’s been about 11 months now, roughly. Special technology… I don’t know that I can prove that. I’m not saying I’ve found a device hidden in the wall or anything like that. What I’m saying is that the way things happen feels coordinated.

The mail being misdelivered, the noises in the walls at certain times, the comments from certain neighbors that seem to line up with things going on in my apartment—it’s hard for me to accept that all of that is just random. And the property manager keeps offering paperwork and explanations like that settles it, but it doesn’t address the pattern.

So if you’re asking, “Do I know there’s some gadget pointed at me?” No, I can’t say that. But I do believe they’re using the building, the mail, the timing of noises, and people around me to put pressure on me and make me want to leave. That’s what has been happening for months.

I moved into the new apartment, and it started not long after that—not necessarily the very first day, but shortly after I got settled enough to notice what was happening.\n\nAt first I thought maybe it was just the usual confusion that comes with a new building, new neighbors, mail getting sorted out, that kind of thing. If you mean something very specific, like a concussion or stroke or something along those lines, then no, not that I’m aware of.\n\nDoctor: Before this apartment situation began, did you generally tend to distrust other people’s motives?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure I’d put it that way. But I wouldn’t say I walked around assuming everyone had bad motives.\n\nBefore the apartment situation, I think I was reasonably cautious, maybe observant. I paid attention to inconsistencies, but I don’t think I was generally distrustful as a person. I had colleagues I could work with, people I could talk to, normal dealings with neighbors and so on.
